title: Ethics and Responsible Technology
description: Changing, stopping, or reshaping technically possible work because of privacy, security, customer trust, fairness, or regulatory risk.

competency.name: Ethics and Responsible Technology
competency.definition: Uses **moral courage**, risk judgment, and practical alternatives when technology decisions affect trust, safety, privacy, or fairness.
competency.whyItMatters: Senior technology leaders are accountable for more than what can be built; they are accountable for what should be built.

prompt.primary: Tell me about a time you stopped or changed a project because of ethical, privacy, security, or customer-trust concerns.
variants: Describe a time when a technically possible solution was not the right thing to build.
Tell me about a time you had to balance product ambition with responsible data use.
interviewerIntent: Does the candidate recognize trust and ethical risk early?
Can they propose alternatives rather than only block?
Do they understand governance, consent, data minimization, and accountability?

scenario.signatureExample: A product team wants to use customer data for personalization, and the CTO requires privacy review, data minimization, consent clarity, and measurable customer benefit.
context: The product idea is commercially attractive.
The proposed implementation uses sensitive customer behavior data.
Legal and security input has not yet been built into the design.
constraints: The leader should not become a reflexive blocker.
Customer trust and compliance risk matter.
The team needs a path to responsible experimentation.

storyAnatomy.situation: A product initiative proposed using customer data in a way that created privacy and trust concerns.
storyAnatomy.task: Protect customers and company trust while preserving a responsible path to **customer value**.
action: Paused the launch until privacy, security, and legal review were included.
Separated the customer benefit from the most invasive implementation.
Required data minimization, consent clarity, retention limits, and abuse-case review.
Defined experiment criteria that measured **customer value** and risk controls.
result: The project moved forward with narrower data use and clearer safeguards.
The product team gained a repeatable responsible-technology review path.
Customer **trust risk** was reduced before launch.
storyAnatomy.reflection: The lesson was that **responsible technology** works best when it creates safer alternatives, not only late-stage objections.

exampleStories.title: Personalization With Data Minimization
exampleStories.promptVariant: Tell me about a time you stopped or changed a project because of privacy or customer-trust concerns.
exampleStories.situation: A product team wanted to use detailed behavioral data for personalization before consent, retention, and customer benefit were clearly defined.
strongAnswerSketch: Pause the launch until privacy, security, legal, and product review are included.
Separate the customer benefit from the most invasive implementation.
Require data minimization, consent clarity, retention limits, and abuse-case review.
Approve a narrower experiment with measurable customer benefit and risk controls.
whyItWorks: Shows **moral courage** without becoming a blocker.
Creates governance for future high-trust-risk decisions.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I asked Legal to review the plan and told Product we should be careful with customer data.
followUpAngles: What data did you remove from scope?

exampleStories.title: AI Fairness Review
exampleStories.promptVariant: Describe a time when a technically possible solution was not the right thing to build.
exampleStories.situation: A ranking model improved aggregate conversion but created worse outcomes for a smaller customer segment and lacked explainability for support teams.
strongAnswerSketch: Name the risk: aggregate metrics hid segment-level harm.
Require segment analysis, explainability, and human override paths before launch.
Work with Product to define acceptable **trade-offs** and customer communication.
whyItWorks: Balances fairness, explainability, and product goals.
Turns a one-off concern into launch criteria.
exampleStories.weakVersion: I delayed the model because we were not confident enough in the fairness implications.
followUpAngles: What became part of future model reviews?

strongAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate shows **moral courage**, practical risk judgment, and ability to guide teams toward safer alternatives.
moves: Names the ethical or **trust risk** concretely.
Explains who was consulted and what governance was needed.

weakAnswerPattern.summary: The candidate either ignores the risk, delegates responsibility entirely, or blocks without helping the team find a responsible path.
redFlags: Treats ethics as legal's problem only.
Cannot explain the **customer harm** or trust risk.
Only says no and offers no alternative.
Has no mechanism for future **responsible technology** decisions.

followUps.question: What specific **customer harm** or trust risk were you concerned about?
Who did you involve in the decision?

signals.name: Trust Risk Judgment
signals.strong: Identifies concrete customer, privacy, security, or fairness risk.
signals.weak: Uses vague concern without actionable risk framing.

signals.name: Moral Courage
signals.strong: Challenges unsafe work even when it has business momentum.
signals.weak: Lets momentum override customer trust concerns.

signals.name: Responsible Alternatives
signals.strong: Finds safer ways to pursue **customer value**.

rubric.expected: Escalates trust risks and applies team-level safeguards.
Coordinates product, legal, security, and engineering decisions for responsible implementation.
Creates governance for high-risk product and data decisions across the organization.
Owns company-level technology trust, ethics posture, and executive decision quality.

prompts.label: What technically possible work created ethical or trust risk?
What customer or company responsibility did you own?
How did you assess risk, involve stakeholders, and propose alternatives?
What changed in the product, decision, or risk posture?
What did you learn about responsible technology leadership?
What governance or review mechanism changed?

relatedScenarios: Changing an AI feature because of fairness or explainability concerns.
Rejecting excessive data collection for personalization.
Delaying launch until security and privacy controls are ready.
